results.blind_working: The zeroth law establishes that thermal equilibrium is transitive. This allows a state function, temperature, to be defined.
For an ideal monatomic gas U = (3/2)nRT, so U is proportional to T. Initial T = 300 K and final T = 600 K, so the ratio is 600/300 = 2.
By the zeroth law, A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other, so they have equal temperatures. Their internal energies and pressures need not be equal, and no net heat flows between them.
R is the zeroth law, which is true. A thermometer acts as the third system, so R correctly explains A.
I is false: a rise of 10°C equals a rise of 10 K. II is false: heat flows from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures are equal, not the internal energies.
Internal energy depends only on the state of the gas. Heat, work and the area under the P-V curve all depend on the path taken.
Work done = area under the linear P-V line = average pressure × change in volume = (2×10^5 Pa)(2×10^-3 m^3) = 400 J.
ΔU = n Cv ΔT for any process. For a diatomic gas Cv = (5/2)R, so ΔU = 2 × 2.5 × 8.3 × 10 = 415 J.
Expansion gives positive work (A-IV). Compression gives negative work (B-II). Constant volume gives zero work (C-I). A clockwise cycle gives positive net work equal to the enclosed area (D-III).
A, B and D are true. C is false because an anticlockwise cycle gives negative net work. E is false because ΔU is path-independent.
By the first law, ΔU = Q − W = 450 − 150 = 300 J, so internal energy increases by 300 J.
At constant pressure, W/Q = nRΔT/(nCpΔT) = R/Cp. For a monatomic gas Cp = 5R/2, so W/Q = 2/5 and W = (2/5)(750) = 300 J.

The gas expands at low pressure and is compressed at high pressure, so the cycle is anticlockwise on a P-V diagram. Net work = −(ΔP)(ΔV) = −(2×10^5)(2×10^-3) = −400 J. Since ΔU = 0 over a cycle, Q = W = −400 J, so 400 J is rejected.
A is true: in an isochoric process W = 0, so Q = ΔU by the first law. R is true, but A follows from W = 0, not from U depending only on temperature. So R does not explain A.
Statement I: for a diatomic gas W/Q = R/Cp = R/(7R/2) = 2/7, which is correct. Statement II: W = nRΔT = 2 × 8.31 × 50 = 831 J, which is correct.
In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so W = -ΔU. Expansion work is positive, so ΔU < 0 and the temperature falls.
W = nRT ln(P1/P2) = 1 × 8.3 × 300 × ln 10 = 2490 × 2.303 ≈ 5734 J ≈ 5.73 kJ, positive because the gas does work on expansion.
Isothermal: ΔT = 0 with Q ≠ 0, so C is infinite (A-II). Adiabatic: Q = 0, so C = 0 (B-III). Adiabatic bulk modulus = γP (C-I). Slope ratio, adiabatic to isothermal = γ (D-IV).

A is false: the isothermal curve lies above the adiabatic, so isothermal work is greater. B is true for a rigid diatomic gas (γ = 7/5). C is true since ΔU = 0, so Q = W. D is true since W = -ΔU = nCv(T1 - T2). E is false: an adiabatic process needs insulating walls or a fast process.
Work per cycle W = 800 - 600 = 200 J. Efficiency = W/Q_hot = 200/800 = 25%.
Heat extracted from the cold body Q_cold = 1000 - 200 = 800 J. COP = Q_cold/W = 800/200 = 4.
For a reversed engine, COP = (1 - η)/η = 0.75/0.25 = 3.
Even with no losses, some heat must be rejected to a cold sink (Kelvin-Planck), so η < 1. A is false and R is true.
I: COP = (1 - η)/η, which increases as η decreases, so I is true. II: Q_hot = Q_cold + W > Q_cold, so II is true.
Efficiency = 1 - T2/T1 = 1 - 300/500 = 0.4, which is 40%.
COP = T2/(T1 - T2) = 250/50 = 5. Minimum work W = Q2/COP = 1000/5 = 200 J.
Heat flowing through a finite temperature difference cannot be reversed by an infinitesimal change, so it is irreversible. The other three processes are ideal reversible ones.

Isothermal expansion absorbs Q1 at T1 (II). Adiabatic expansion lowers the temperature from T1 to T2 (IV). Isothermal compression rejects Q2 at T2 (III). Adiabatic compression raises the temperature from T2 to T1 (I).

A is false: Carnot efficiency is independent of the working substance. B is true by Carnot's theorem. C is true: free expansion is irreversible. D is true: a reversible process must be quasi-static and free of dissipation. E is false: 0°C is 273 K, not 0 K, so efficiency is below 100%.
